analysis.one_liner: Caps voter wait times at 30 minutes in federal elections and lets voters sue over long lines.
analysis.headline: Senator Wyden's bill to cap voting lines at 30 minutes, fine states for long waits, and bar election officials from running campaigns died in the Senate Rules Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Help America Vote Act to guarantee that no voter waits more than 30 minutes to vote in a federal election. States that failed would face lawsuits from voters, with penalties starting at $50 plus $50 per extra hour waited, and much larger penalties for deliberate vote suppression. It also would have required federal standards for the minimum number of voting machines and poll workers at each polling place, sent states up to $500 million a year to meet the requirements, and banned chief state election officials from campaigning in federal elections they oversee.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters — especially in predominantly Black, Latino, and low-income neighborhoods where studies cited in the bill show lines run longest — would gain a legally enforceable right to vote without long waits. Voters who wait too long could collect monetary penalties from the state, and emergency paper ballots would be required when machines fail. States would receive federal money to hire poll workers and buy equipment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters stuck in long lines, especially voters of color

how_it_helps.text: Each state must ensure no voter waits more than 30 minutes at any polling place in a federal election, and must submit a public plan describing how it will achieve equal wait times.

Voters who wait longer can sue and recover $50 plus $50 per additional hour, attorney's fees, and up to $650 plus $150 per hour if the court finds the delay was an intentional effort to suppress votes or showed reckless disregard.

The Justice Department must issue uniform standards for the minimum number and distribution of voting systems, poll workers, and other election resources, factoring in turnout, registration, disability access, and language needs, to equalize wait times across communities.

States are authorized to receive $500 million per year in federal payments to fund the resources needed to meet the requirements, and voters must be offered emergency paper ballots when machines fail.

Chief state election administration officials are barred from taking an active part in political campaigns for federal elections they supervise, including fundraising for candidates, unless they fully recuse themselves.

analysis.who_pays: States would bear the cost of meeting the 30-minute standard, with federal payments authorized but subject to annual appropriations, and would face civil penalties through voter lawsuits when they fall short. Chief election officials would lose the ability to campaign or fundraise while overseeing elections they supervise.

drawbacks.text: The private right of action could generate substantial litigation against states after every federal election, since the bill lets any aggrieved voter sue and collect attorney's fees from the state.

The $500 million annual payments are authorized but not guaranteed — Congress would still have to appropriate the money each year, so states could face binding federal mandates without matching funding.

Federal minimum-resource standards and Commission-imposed remedial plans for states with waits over 60 minutes would shift control over election administration, historically run by states and counties, toward Washington.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete and enforceable: a court-backed right to vote without multi-hour lines, aimed directly at documented racial disparities in wait times. The costs are real but mostly fiscal and administrative for states, and the federal money in the bill is designed to offset them. The main design risk is litigation exposure and the possibility that appropriated funds fall short of the mandate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the People Over Long Lines Act on June 17, 2021, for himself and Senator Jeff Merkley, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day.
Merckley was the bill's only cosponsor; no other senator joined in the entire two-year Congress.
The Committee on Rules and Administration took no action on the bill — no hearing, no committee vote — and it never reached the Senate floor.

The bill's findings cite research showing voters in predominantly Black neighborhoods waited 29 percent longer on average than those in white neighborhoods, and that long lines deterred an estimated 500,000 to 700,000 voters in 2012.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State election offices and incumbent officials who would have faced new federal mandates, lawsuits from voters, and a ban on campaigning while overseeing elections are better off because the bill died. Voters in long-line communities gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State election officials who avoided new mandates

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing or markup — so it never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators ever sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it never came to a vote, so the partisan shape of opposition was never tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Voting equipment manufacturers and election services vendors
industries.note: The bill requires states to provide minimum numbers of voting systems and poll workers at every polling place and authorizes $500 million a year in federal payments to buy those resources, which would flow heavily to election technology suppliers. Ordinary voters share the benefit through shorter lines.

industries.industry: Chief state election administration officials (secretaries of state and equivalents)
industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful for the top state election official to take an active part in federal political campaigns they supervise, including fundraising and using official authority to affect an election's result, unless they recuse. This closes a route by which officials can run races they administer.

States would gain federal grants to fund election administration but also take on binding wait-time limits, federal resource standards, Commission-imposed remedial plans for chronic long waits, and exposure to voter lawsuits with attorney's fees.
